title: Verbs of the Mind and the Page

lessons.title: думать (dúmat') — "to think"
lessons.gloss: to think — and the fact that shapes every Russian verb you will ever meet

segments.text: Six verbs behind you. This one opens the largest fact about Russian verbs.

blocks.title: You'll want to know first — думать

segments.text: думать — dúmat' — to think.
No new letters, and the -ть of znat'. Stress on the first syllable, and it never moves: DOO-mat'.
ya dúmayu — I think.
That -ю is the one you put on znáyu. And ty dúmayesh — an -yesh, so думать (dúmat') files with znat', not говорить.
Three verbs of the head now: ya znáyu is a fact I hold, ya vízhu is what reaches my eyes, я думаю is what goes on behind them.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: every Russian verb travels with a partner

segments.text: Russian verbs come in pairs. One member is the doing — under way, repeated, unfinished. The other is the deed done, seen whole.
Думать is the first kind; its partner подумать is not "to think" but "to have a thought, and be done with it."

You have met the instinct once. Идти was going now, one way, with a separate partner for going as a habit — one small family of motion verbs. This is a different distinction, applied to nearly every verb in the language.
So one job per verb: learn its partner's name. What a pair does to a sentence is a later lesson.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — a thought, and a parliament

segments.text: дума is the Russian noun for a thought — and for a body that thinks: the State Дума is the lower house of the Russian parliament, this same word.

Its own origin carries a hedge. The standard account makes дума an early borrowing from Gothic dōms, "a judgement" — behind English doom (a judgement before it was a fate) and deem. If so, думать (dúmat') and doom are relatives by contact, not by descent; a minority prefer an inherited root.
Latin's cogito, ergo sum is built on the same idea, and its other pieces are yours: the -o of cogito is Latin ego, the pronoun Russian keeps as я; and fuī, "I was," is byt''s root, English be.

segments.text: Say "I think." (Ya dúmayu.) Which family does думать (dúmat') join, znáyesh or gavarísh? (Znáyesh.) What is подумать beside думать (dúmat'), and how many verbs have such a partner? (The finished member; nearly all.) Which English word does the standard account attach дума to? (Doom, by borrowing.)

lessons.title: понимать (ponimát') — "to understand"
lessons.gloss: to understand — literally to take hold of, which is what comprehend means too

segments.text: The most useful sentence a traveller owns is short, and after this lesson it is yours: I don't understand.

blocks.title: You'll want to know first — понимать

segments.text: понимать — ponimát' — to understand.
No new letters. Stress on the last syllable, and both оs lean towards a away from it: pa-ni-MAT'.
ya panimáyu — I understand.
The same -ю as dúmayu. And now the sentence worth more than the rest:
ya ne panimáyu — I don't understand.
Не does the whole job, exactly as in ya ne znáyu: one word in front of the verb, no helper borrowed from anywhere. Say those syllables to a Russian speaker and the conversation slows down for you.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the partner, and a warning about its shape

segments.text: Dúmat' took podúmat': a prefix on the front, nothing else disturbed. Do not expect that every time.

Понимать's partner is понять — same root, but the middle of the word has been squeezed out, -ним- against -ня-. Russian builds a pair by prefix, by a reshaped stem, or by both, and the shape is learned with the verb.
The job is unchanged: понимать (ponimát'), понять, said together, one entry.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — understanding is a kind of grabbing

segments.text: понимать (ponimát') is по- plus a root meaning simply to take: Indo-European h₁em-, which came down the Latin branch as emere, "to take, and so to buy." English took the family whole — exempt (taken out), redeem (bought back), example (taken as a specimen), premium, prompt, assume, consume.

So понимать (ponimát') literally says take hold of. English says the same and has stopped noticing: comprehend is Latin com-prehendere, "to seize together"; grasp is what a hand does; German begreifen is greifen, "to grip."

Set that beside the two pictures Russian already gave you. Znat' was ǵneh₃-, English know — knowledge you simply have. Видеть was weid-, which meant see and know at once and gave English wit and wise — knowledge you saw. Now understanding as something you caught. And unlike dúmat', which arrived by Gothic borrowing, this one is inherited straight down.

segments.instruction: "понимать (ponimát')" — pa-ni-MAT', both os leaning to a
"Ya panimáyu" then "Ya ne panimáyu" — one word added, nothing else

segments.text: Say "I don't understand." (Ya ne panimáyu.) Name понимать (ponimát')'s partner and say how its shape differs from podúmat'. (Понять — the stem is reshaped, not just prefixed.) What does the root of понимать (ponimát') mean? (To take — as comprehend and grasp also do.) And which of your knowing-verbs is a borrowing rather than an inheritance? (Dúmat', from Gothic.)

lessons.title: читать (chitát') — "to read"
lessons.gloss: to read — and why Russian has no separate way to say I am reading

segments.text: English says I read and I am reading and means two things. Russian cannot — and the reason is a verb it refuses to say.

blocks.title: You'll want to know first — читать

segments.text: читать — chitát' — to read.
No new letters: ч you have been reading since очень, and it says the ch of cheese. Stress on the last syllable, chi-TAT'.
ya chitáyu — I read.
The same -ю, and ty chitáyesh puts it with znat' and dúmat'. Two verbs, one ordinary sentence:
ya chitáyu i panimáyu — I read and I understand.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: one present tense, two English sentences

segments.text: Ya chitáyu is I read and I am reading. Russian has one present tense and it covers both.

There is a reason, and you hold it. English builds I am reading out of be plus -ing; Russian's byt' has no present tense to build with — the missing verb of Chapter 3, the one Ya studént does without. With no auxiliary, Russian never grew the machinery.
The work English does with am reading against read is carried instead by the pair. Chitát' is the ongoing member; прочитать is the finished one — to read a thing through, to the end.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — reading, honour, and counting

segments.text: читать (chitát') rests on an old Slavic root meaning to count, to reckon, to heed, and Russian keeps the family in plain sight: chisló is a number, честь is honour, почитать is to hold in esteem. Counting, respecting and reading are one act — careful attention, item by item. Outside Slavic the root surfaces in Sanskrit cétati, "he perceives."

And then the trail stops. There is no secure English descendant, and the two words that look promising are not it: cheat is a clipped escheat, from Latin cadere, "to fall," and chit, the little note, came into English from India. This book would rather hand you nothing than a cousin that is only a resemblance — the care it took with говорить, which is not govern.

segments.instruction: "Ya chitáyu i panimáyu" — and hear it as both read and am reading
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "Ya chitáyu i panimáyu" — and hear it as both *read* and *am reading*]

segments.instruction: the pair — "читать (chitát') … прочитать", the doing and the read-through
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the pair — "читать … прочитать", the doing and the read-through]

segments.text: Say "I read and I understand." (Ya chitáyu i panimáyu.) Give the two English sentences я читаю covers, and say why. (I read and I am reading; byt' has no present tense to build the second.) Name the finished partner. (Прочитать.) Which two Russian nouns share this root, and is читать (chitát') related to English cheat? (Chisló and честь; and no — as говорить was not related to govern.)

lessons.title: писать (pisát') — "to write"
lessons.gloss: to write — one new letter, and the one stress mistake you must not make

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: you can do this one in the car, but part of it needs your eyes. For that part you will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now. I will say so again when we reach it, but leave this section until you have stopped: The letters in this word.

segments.text: A new letter, an English family you know on sight, and a stress mistake worth naming before you make it.

blocks.title: You'll want to know first — писать

segments.text: писать — pisát' — to write.
Stress on the last syllable, pi-SAT' — not a detail you may skip.
ya pishú — I write, and I am writing.

Two things moved: the с becomes sh in the present, and the stress that sat on the ending for I jumps back to the stem elsewhere — pishú, but ty píshesh. The pair runs as it did for chitát': писать (pisát') ongoing, написать finished.

Careful. Писать stressed at the end — pisát' — is to write. Писать stressed at the front — písat' — is a child's word for to urinate, whose I form is písayu beside pishú. The two differ only in where your voice lifts, and beginners land on the wrong one. Stress the end and say pishú.
(Skim if you read Cyrillic.) All of писать (pisát') is familiar; the new sound arrives in pishú.
"sh", the sound of shoe, has a letter of its own: three uprights on a bar, like a comb with the teeth up. You will write it in the letter chapters.

You have been hearing it without being told: zhivyósh, znáyesh, gavarísh and the past shol all carry it. And note the kind of letter it is: я lies to a Latin reader, looking like a mirrored R while being a vowel; the comb resembles nothing Latin at all.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — writing was scratching

segments.text: писать (pisát') is Indo-European peyḱ-, "to cut, to scratch, to mark" — before ink there was a point and a surface. The root became, in Latin, pingere, "to paint", and English took the results: paint, picture, pigment. Russian's pis'mó (a letter) and pisátel' (a writer) sit on the verb.

That closes the chapter's thread: dúmat' came in from Gothic, ponimát' is a root meaning take, chitát' a root meaning count with no English descendant, and писать (pisát') a root meaning scratch that handed English a wall of paint.

segments.text: Say "I write." (Ya pishú.) Where does the stress go, and what if it goes on the front? (On the end; písat' is a child's word for urinating.) What sound does the comb-shaped letter make? (Sh — zhivyósh, znáyesh, gavarísh, shol.) Say the chapter's four verbs in the I form, then their finished partners. (Ya dúmayu, ya panimáyu, ya chitáyu, ya pishú; podúmat', понять, prochitát', написать.) And what did писать (pisát')'s root mean? (To scratch — hence paint.)
